transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my lieutenant... he's the one who made me come down here. I didn't even think I needed to leave the station, to be honest with you. See, I was just in the apparatus bay, right by the rigs. I'm an EMT, so I know the gear, I know how things are supposed to be. But I was looking at the airway bags, and they just... they weren't right. So I started moving them. I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern, because I just knew, I knew it was the exact right way they had to sit. It’s like a grid, almost, and it had to be perfect. And while I was doing it, I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, just saying them over and over so the rhythm matched the way I was setting the bags down. 

Then my lieutenant comes walking up, and he's telling me to stop. He's saying to step away from the bags, step away from the rig, but I couldn't. I wouldn't step away. He didn't understand what was happening, and he started getting kind of loud about it. I tried to make him see that I couldn't just stop in the middle of it. If I broke the sequence right then, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. Like the concrete, the trucks, the air, the whole station—everything would just go completely bad if I didn't finish the pattern with the numbers. But he wouldn't listen to me, he just pulled me off shift and told me I had to come see you.

Well, see, the thing with the bags, that specific thing... I mean, it's not just the bags, it's the paperwork too. The run reports, the incident logs, the way they have to be stacked, the way the edges have to line up exactly parallel to the desk. If they aren't, the information gets... it gets contaminated. And the cameras, too. The security cameras at the station and the dashcams in the rigs. I started noticing them differently, you know? Like they were recording the wrong frequencies or something, so I had to start covering certain ones up or standing at very specific angles so they wouldn't mess with my head while I was trying to get the paperwork right. All of that—the cameras, the paperwork, the bags in the bay, everything that made the lieutenant so upset—it's all been happening for about two months now. Give or take a few days, but right around two months. Before that, things were fine, mostly fine, but these last two months, it's just been so clear to me how everything is connected and how careful I have to be with the arrangements. If I don't do it, I don't know who will, and then what happens to the station? It's a lot of responsibility, and I don't think they understand how crucial it's been these past eight weeks.
During these past two months, have you felt like you need much less sleep than usual to feel rested and energized?

Sleep? No, I wouldn't say I feel energized. I mean, I'm definitely sleeping, but it's not like I'm bouncing off the walls or anything. I just... I try to get my rest when I can, you know? But the thing is, even when I'm lying there in my bunk at the station, or at home in my own bed, my mind is still going over the grid. The patterns. I can close my eyes, but I still see the airway bags, and I still hear the dispatch numbers ticking away in my head like a metronome. Tick, tick, tick, one-four-niner, two-seven-six. So, I do sleep, I get my hours in, mostly, but the resting part? I don't know if you could call it restful because the responsibility doesn't stop just because I close my eyes. If I'm asleep, who's making sure the frequencies from the cameras aren't bleeding into the incident logs? Nobody, that's who. So I wake up and I feel this weight, this heaviness, like I've been working a double shift just trying to keep the station from falling apart while I was unconscious. But no, I don't feel energized on less sleep, I just feel like there's never enough time to get everything aligned the way it absolutely has to be.
Do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people can't hear when no one is around?

Voices? No, no, I don't hear people talking to me when nobody's there. I mean, I told you about the dispatch numbers, right? I hear those, but that's me, that's my own head keeping the rhythm, keeping the sequence going. It's not like some stranger whispering in the corner of the room or anything like that. But, you know, the sounds... the frequencies I mentioned before with the cameras? That's a different thing entirely. It's not a voice, it's more like a... like a hum. A low, vibrating hum that just gets under my skin. 

I first noticed it when I was trying to align the run reports. I was sitting at the desk, making sure the edges were perfectly parallel, and I just felt this vibration in my teeth. It was coming from the security camera up in the corner of the dayroom. And nobody else seemed to notice! The other guys were just watching TV, eating dinner, totally oblivious to the fact that this camera was putting out this... this interference. It's not a voice, but it's a sound, a frequency that messes with the alignment of everything. And it's not just the cameras, sometimes it's the fluorescent lights in the bay, or the radio static when it's just sitting there on the charger. It's like they're all humming at this wrong pitch, and if I don't correct the pattern, if I don't move the bags or stack the papers right, that hum is going to just shatter everything. But actual voices? Like someone saying, 'Hey, do this' or 'Do that'? No, I don't get that. It's just the hum, the frequencies, and the dispatch numbers that I have to repeat to keep the hum from taking over the station.
Do you believe someone is deliberately using those cameras and frequencies to watch you or interfere with your mind?

Well, see, that's the thing. That's exactly the thing I've been trying to explain to the lieutenant, but he just looks at me like I'm crazy. It's not just a random hum, you know? It's not just some electrical glitch. I know exactly what's happening. It's the injury review board. The injury review people and some of the upper supervisors, the ones who sit in the downtown office and never actually run a call. They're the ones using the cameras. They've got them calibrated to put out that frequency, and they're watching me. Specifically me. 

I started putting it together a few weeks ago when I was doing my triage notes. I'm always meticulous with my notes, you have to be, right? But I'd go back into the system, and things were changed. A respiratory rate would be off by two breaths, or the Glasgow Coma Scale would be documented wrong. And I know I didn't write it that way. I know the exact sequence of numbers I typed. But they're going in, through the system, while they're watching me on the cameras, and they're altering my reports. 

They tell me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork audits, everyone gets them." Routine! There's nothing routine about it. They're deliberately changing my triage notes to make me look incompetent, to make me look unsafe on the rig. That's why the frequencies are so strong when I'm doing the paperwork. They're trying to disrupt my thought process, trying to scramble the grid in my head so I won't notice what they're doing to the files. That's why I have to align the edges of the papers perfectly, to create a sort of... a barrier, I guess, against the interference. But yeah, they are absolutely doing it on purpose. They sit there watching the feeds, tweaking the frequencies, messing with my notes, all to build this fake case against me. It's so obvious if you just look at the patterns, but nobody else at the station wants to see it. They just think I'm being difficult about the bags and the cameras, but I'm the only one who actually sees what the supervisors are up to.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with prominent persecutory delusions and delusions of control/influence involving workplace supervisors and camera frequencies affecting his thoughts, files, and physical sensations. These delusional beliefs have led to secondary ritualistic and bizarre behaviors (arranging gear, chanting numbers to counteract frequencies). Symptoms have persisted continuously for approximately two months (exceeding the one-month duration criterion for ICD-10 schizophrenia), causing acute occupational impairment, and are not secondary to a mood episode or substance use.
